Wir wollen indessen das Hauptgesetz hier gleich anführen, weil wir im Folgenden die Wirkungen des Accentes näher besprechen werden. Es lautet folgendermassen: „Der Hauptaccent ist immer auf der ersten Silbe des Wortes, der Nebenaccent aber gewöhnlich auf der 3:ten, 5:ten, 7:ten u. s. v. oder, besonders wenn in einem 5- oder mehr als 5- silbigen Worte die dritte Silbe auf einen kurzen Vocal auslautet, auf der 4:ten, 6:ten, 8:ten u. s. v., niemals aber auf der zweiten noch letzten Silbe des Wortes.“ Kleinere Abweichungen trifft man bisweilen in den Fremdwörtern, z. new_statements.quote: Stress in Soikkola Ingrian has been scarcely studied (Porkka, 1885, pp. 36–37; Laanest, 1993, p. 57; Gordon, 2009). Early authors described it as a general Finnic system (first proposed for Finnish by Genetz, 1881) with primary stress on the word-initial syllable and secondary stresses on subsequent odd syllables apart from the final one. However, the general structure of metrical prominence in Finnic languages is still under-researched. Based on our earlier observations (Kuznecova, 2009b, 2009a), we describe the stress system of Soikkola Ingrian as similar to that of Estonian (viz. Kuznetsova, 2018a). The lowest type of metrical prominence is foot-initial stress.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's initial-stress rule (initial stress = stress on syllable 1 at every length): primary stress is word-initial. Adds the foot-based analysis, the odd-syllable secondary stresses, lexicalised suffix accents, variable rhythmic footing in longer words, and the durational/pitch correlates. Describes only the Soikkola dialect (north subdialect), one of four Ingrian dialects.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the word-initial syllable (the traditional Finnic description, which the authors do not dispute for the primary stress); the authors recast the system as foot-based like Estonian: every foot (trochaic or dactylic) has foot-initial stress cued by duration (no reduction/shortening of the stressed vowel, 'half-long' V2 in light feet, V2 reduction in heavy feet) and by high pitch anchored on the foot-initial syllable. Word-initial syllable = first foot head, hence primary stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Traditional account: secondary stresses on subsequent odd syllables except the final one. Authors' account (p. 3): foot stress is either lexicalised (phonological accent bound to certain morphemes: roots and some inflectional/derivational affixes, marked /´/, cannot shift) or rhythmic; stretches longer than two syllables between lexicalised accents are divided into mostly trochaic and dactylic feet, and 'The placement of rhythmic stresses is to a certain degree variable in multifoot words (viz. Kuznecova, 2009b)', e.g. ´naise´likkaha(l̆)le 'married:ALL' [ˈnai̯ʒĕˌlikːăˌhałˑe] ~ [ˈnai̯ʒĕˌlikːăcăˌłeˑ]. Section 6.3 (p. 16-17): 'Secondary stressed feet can also entirely lose stress in speech'; variable rhythmic stress also yields variable secondary gemination (´opastajoja ~ ´opastaj̆joja 'teacher:PL:PRT').
new_statements.exceptions: Some suffixes carry a lexicalised accent (e.g. ´-likka-), so a non-initial secondary stress can be fixed to a suffix rather than counted rhythmically; rhythmic secondary stress placement varies between speakers/tokens; pitch marking of prominence may be post-lexical (accentual phrase level) rather than word-level (citing Gordon 2009, pp. 98-99), and the authors call foot stress 'a more robust phenomenon than word-level stress'.
new_statements.identity_note: Kuznetsova, Brodskaya & Markus 2023 describes Soikkola Ingrian, north subdialect (speakers from the Soikkola peninsula, Leningrad oblast), one of four Ingrian dialects (Soikkola, Lower Luga, extinct Hevaha and Oredež). The wrongly-resolved item for work 0 (Markus & Rozhanskiy 2023, JEFUL) is likewise on Soikkola Ingrian. No source opened here covers Lower Luga Ingrian.
